title: Faith, with open hands. — Aaron Alderman
description: A personal Christian reading of God, Jesus, the Bible, Christianity and other religions, with room for careful interpretation and honest disagreement.

children: AARON ALDERMAN / FAITH & INTERPRETATION
Faith, with open hands.
How I read God, Jesus, the Bible and other religions.
A personal theological essay · A working reading, open to correction

attrs.alt: An imagined open Bible rests on a stone table beneath an olive tree in warm morning light.

children: I want a faith that can look closely: at Jesus, at a difficult passage, at another person, and at the harm done in God’s name. I also want room for worship, prayer and hope. Careful interpretation belongs inside that life.

The reading behind this corpus begins with a conviction: power should serve life, and Jesus gives that conviction its Christian centre. What follows is an account of that reading. I am responsible for its choices; calling them Christian does not make them the only Christian choices.

What do I mean by God?

When I say God, I mean the source and sustainer of life, worthy of trust and worship because of goodness as well as power. The question is therefore moral as well as metaphysical: what kind of power deserves our love?

The kenotic account developed here understands divine power through self-giving love. Kenosis means self-emptying: using power in a way that makes room for another person’s life and agency. In this reading, love can restrain power and can also require protection, judgment or intervention. Leaving someone exposed to domination would fail that purpose.

That is a theological proposal. It does not follow from a physics equation, a beautiful landscape or a successful computer model. Nor does it explain away cruelty, disaster or the experience of a sincere person who seeks God and finds silence. Those remain difficult questions for this faith to face.
Read the corpus’s challenge about divine hiddenness.
Why begin with Jesus?

For this Christian reading, Jesus is the centre by which I try to understand the character of God. John’s account of God entering human life, the self-giving described in Philippians, and Jesus’ teaching about serving others guide the interpretation. These are particular Christian commitments, with historical and theological claims that deserve their own examination.
See the scriptural starting points.

Incarnation means God entering embodied human life: dependence, vulnerability, relationships, suffering. The cross brings the question of power into the presence of violence. Resurrection carries the Christian hope that violence and death do not have the final word. I cannot reduce that hope to a metaphor for feeling better, or treat a moving moral story as proof that the resurrection happened.

Self-giving also needs careful handling. Jesus’ service cannot become an instruction for a person with less power to disappear, accept abuse or keep an institution comfortable. The question belongs first to those who hold power: what must I relinquish so someone else can live more freely? A protective boundary can be an act of love.
How do I read the Bible?

I approach scripture as a collection of writings to be read carefully, in their literary and historical settings, within the larger Christian story. A lament, a proverb, a parable, a law and a letter do different kinds of work. Identifying who is speaking, to whom and in what circumstances comes before turning a sentence into an instruction for today.

Reading through Jesus means taking his account of love of God and neighbour seriously when interpreting the rest. It also requires honesty about the choice I am making. Christians disagree about how scripture, tradition, reason and experience should relate. A Christ-centred reading still has to account for the passages it finds difficult; it cannot quietly remove them.
Matthew 22:34–40 is an important starting point.
Five questions beside an open Bible
What does the passage actually say, and what am I adding?
What kind of writing is this, and who first heard it?
How does this reading sit with the life and teaching of Jesus?
Who bears the cost if I act on it—and have I listened to them?
What evidence or better reading would make me revise my view?

These questions take time. Comparing translations, reading the surrounding chapter, listening to informed disagreement and learning from people affected by a teaching can all expose something I missed. Difficulty is a reason to read more carefully. I should be able to say where the text ends and my interpretation begins.
How do I understand Christianity?

Christianity is a lived, varied tradition of worship, prayer, community, teaching and action, centred on Jesus Christ. A Christian life involves belonging, receiving and practising, as well as making claims about what is true. Its churches and traditions carry gifts and disagreements; their history also includes grave failures.

The corpus develops one kenotic reading within that wider tradition. It draws together self-giving, service, participation and hope. Its own theological audit rejects the claim that this is the uniquely necessary interpretation of Christianity. I should make that limit visible, especially when these ideas inform the software and institutions I build.
Read why this remains one Christian reading.

I want to ask what a teaching produces in practice: truthfulness, costly care, protection of the vulnerable, a willingness to repair harm. That examination must include Christian failures and goodness outside Christianity. Good consequences matter, but they cannot by themselves establish a religion’s historical or metaphysical claims. Equally, calling harm a spiritual lesson does not make the harm acceptable.
Read the distinction between fruit, harm and truth.
How do I meet other religions?

I can begin from a Christian commitment and still encounter another tradition with patience and respect. I need to learn what its people actually believe and practise, including disagreements within the tradition. Judaism, Islam, Buddhist and Hindu traditions, other faiths and nonreligious ways of life deserve more than a role in a Christian argument.

I should resist flattening these traditions into interchangeable versions of my own. Their accounts of God, ultimate reality, liberation, salvation and human purpose can differ substantially. Respect allows those differences to remain visible. It also asks me to describe another person’s position in terms they can recognise before I judge it.

Shared compassion, disciplined attention or personal transformation can reveal important human possibilities. They do not automatically settle incompatible religious claims. The corpus makes this point explicitly: similar outcomes can have several explanations. I must apply the same care to a Christian experience as to an experience in another tradition.
Read the corpus’s comparative boundary.

I do not have to settle every ultimate question before treating someone as a neighbour. I can listen, work alongside them, receive correction and acknowledge goodness without asking them to become a supporting character in my account of God. An honest disagreement can remain an honest relationship.
What changes in an ordinary decision?

Suppose a person with authority says that faith requires someone else to stay silent about harm. Before accepting that claim, I should ask for the passage and its context, examine how the authority is being used, and listen to the person carrying the cost. Their safety and freedom to speak need attention now.

The practical movement is simple to name and demanding to live: slow down, distinguish the text from the interpretation, hear the people involved, ask what love and protection require, act within the authority I actually have, and remain answerable for what follows.

Prayer, a trusted community and careful study can belong in that process. So can evidence, disagreement and professional help where needed. A model can make assumptions and possible consequences more visible. Responsibility for a real person stays with us.
